items.title: The 4Ds: vague prompt to verified report
items.text:
"Help me with reports" is not a prompt. It is a wish.

Day 1: Maya asks Claude for help with reports and gets generic structure tips. The video walks her through the 4Ds: Description, Delegation, Discernment and Diligence.

She tells her manager what Claude does and where it stops, hands the metrics draft to Claude but keeps the renewal-risk call herself, and runs her checklist on every output, even the low-stakes ones.

The takeaway: fluency is a habit around the tool, not a clever prompt. The 4Ds are the largest domain on the CCAS-F (Claude Certified Associate – Foundations) exam.

items.title: Discovery to ADR: the SLA gate decides first
items.text:
The higher-quality architecture lost. It missed the latency SLA.

Week 1: the CFO budgets $2.4M and gives you eight weeks. Discovery comes first, not a prototype, and the clinical team names two hard constraints.

Architecture X scores higher on quality but averages 4.2s, so the SLA gate drops it. Architecture Y clears the gate at 2.1s, and only survivors are compared on cost. ADR-07 records the decision.

The takeaway: hard constraints filter before anything is scored. Business value, SLAs and discovery make up a full CCAR-P domain.

items.title: Artifacts: the procedure gets a permanent home
items.text:
Your best procedure is buried 30 turns up in a chat. That is where it goes to die.

Maya asks Claude for a 10-step client onboarding procedure. It lands in chat, and 30 turns later it is lost in scrollback.

A colleague shows her Artifacts. She asks again, Claude judges the content reusable and renders it in the side panel, apart from the conversation. Two days later it is still there to reuse.

The takeaway: chat is for conversation, Artifacts are for things you will keep. Knowing when Claude creates one is classic CCAS-F material.

items.title: Messages API: your first call, every token counted
items.text:
Most first Claude API calls put the instructions in the wrong place.

Day 1: the ticket classifier leaves its notebook and becomes a service. You pick Sonnet for real-time triage, set max_tokens, and call messages.create().

The exam trap the video dodges: behaviour belongs in the system prompt; the user turn carries only the ticket. Then every token in and out is counted.

The takeaway: model, max_tokens, system and messages each have a job. Getting this anatomy right is foundational for the Claude Certified Developer – Foundations (CCDV-F).

items.title: Prompt structure: four elements, one consistent answer
items.text:
Same file. Same prompt. Three completely different answers. Why?

Maya uploads a 20-page contract and types "Summarize this." Run 1 gives a 3-sentence overview, run 2 a 2-page bullet list, run 3 a table.

Her manager spots the gap: she said what, but not who it is for, why, or in what format. Maya rewrites with a role, context, task and format, and the answers become consistent.

The takeaway: when you leave blanks, Claude fills them, differently each time. This four-element structure shows up across the CCAS-F exam.

The CCAS-F prep course covers prompting in depth, with a practice exam at the end:

items.title: Agent SDK: query() runs the loop for you
items.text:
On the plain Messages API, you write the agent loop. With the Agent SDK, you do not.

Your app calls query() once with a prompt and options: Glob, Grep, Read, max_turns=8. Claude returns a tool_use block.

Normally your code would detect it, run it and loop. Here the SDK does it: hooks, then deny rules, then allow rules, then can_use_tool, and only then the tool runs.

The takeaway: knowing that evaluation order is half of the CCAR-F (Claude Certified Architect – Foundations) SDK domain.

Start the CCAR-F prep course, with a practice exam:
👉 https://gennoor.com/claude/certifications/architect-foundations

items.title: AsyncAnthropic: three tickets in flight at once
items.text:
Three tickets arrived at once. Two of them timed out waiting for the first.

Traffic spikes and the sync Flask service sends ticket 1, then blocks while it waits. Tickets 2 and 3 sit idle until their requests time out.

Switching to AsyncAnthropic makes every call awaitable, and asyncio.gather() keeps all three in flight at once.

The takeaway: under concurrent load, a blocking client is the bottleneck, not the model. Async architecture is part of the CCDV-F SDK domain.

🔊 Turn the sound on for the walkthrough.

items.title: ClaudeAgentOptions: deny always beats allow
items.text:
You allowed Read and Grep. Claude still asked for Bash. That is expected.

ClaudeAgentOptions allows Read and Grep, denies Bash, and caps the run at 10 turns. Claude asks for Bash anyway.

Why? allowed_tools approves tools; it does not hide the others. The SDK refuses the call before anything runs, because a deny rule always beats an allow, and Claude turns to an allowed tool.

The takeaway: allow lists grant, deny lists enforce. A favourite CCAR-F exam distinction.

🔊 Turn the sound on for the walkthrough.

items.title: Batch API: 10K tickets overnight, half price
items.text:
If nobody is waiting for the answer, why pay real-time prices?

Finance asks whether the overnight 10K-ticket classification job can cost less. Real-time calls would answer instantly at full price, with nobody waiting.

Instead, at 8pm all 10K tickets go into one batch, each tagged with a custom_id. TicketFlow polls batches.retrieve() and by 6am the results are back, at half price.

The takeaway: match latency to need. The Batch API is a classic cost question on the Claude Certified Developer – Foundations (CCDV-F) exam.

See the cost chapters in the CCDV-F prep course, with a practice exam:
👉 https://gennoor.com/claude/certifications/developer-foundations

items.title: Tool lifecycle: Claude asks, your @tool answers
items.text:
Claude never touches your inventory system. It asks, and your function answers.

Your code registers check_stock as an in-process @tool and asks about SKU A-100. Claude reads the tool description and emits a ToolUseBlock.

Hooks run, the permission check passes, and the SDK calls your function in-process. The result returns as a ToolResultBlock, and Claude answers with the real figure.

The takeaway: the tool description drives the request, your code owns the execution. Core material for the Claude Certified Architect – Foundations (CCAR-F).

The CCAR-F prep course covers tools and MCP in depth, with a practice exam:
👉 https://gennoor.com/claude/certifications/architect-foundations

items.title: RBAC at retrieval: filter by role before the prompt
items.text:
If a billing clerk's query pulls diagnoses into the prompt, the model is not your problem.

A billing clerk asks which procedure codes were billed for a patient. The wrong design uses a shared token and pulls every match, diagnoses included, into the prompt.

The right design passes the clerk's own identity, and retrieval applies the ACL filter inside the vector DB query, so only billing and demographic data ever reaches Claude.

The takeaway: enforce access before the prompt, never after the answer. RAG and RBAC is the heaviest-weighted CCAR-P domain.

🔊 Turn the sound on for the walkthrough.

items.title: MCP: discover over two transports, call by name
items.text:
One MCP server runs as a local subprocess, the other over HTTP. Claude cannot tell.

Your code lists two mcp_servers: fs over stdio and crm as a remote server. The SDK is the MCP client: it spawns fs locally and connects to crm remotely, asking each for tools/list.

Tools are named mcp__<server>__<tool>, and allowed_tools decides which Claude may use. Then Claude calls them by name.

The takeaway: transport is a deployment detail, discovery and naming are the contract. Expect both on the CCAR-F exam.

🔊 Turn the sound on for the walkthrough.

items.title: Prompt caching: pay for the filing once
items.text:
Legal sent the same 80-page filing 14 times, and paid for it 14 times.

Meridian is $840k over budget. Each query bills 40k fresh input tokens: 560k tokens per case.

You reorder the prompt so the filing comes first, marked cache_control: ephemeral. Query 1 writes the prefix to the cache; queries 2 to 14 read it at a fraction of the price.

The takeaway: put the stable content first and cache it. Token-lifecycle cost questions like this are core to the Claude Certified Architect – Professional (CCAR-P).

items.title: Prompt caching: write once, read at 90% off
items.text:
Every agent turn re-sent the same 10K-token knowledge base at full price.

Costs spike because each turn ships the static KB again. You mark that system block with cache_control: ephemeral.

Turn 1 is a cache miss: Claude writes the KB to the cache with a small write fee. Turn 2 sends the identical block, same model, exact prefix, and the cache hits; only the new input is billed in full.

The takeaway: cache what does not change and keep the prefix identical. Cache hit and miss rules are fair game on the CCDV-F exam.

🔊 Turn the sound on for the walkthrough.

items.title: Subagents: the memo returns, not the notebook
items.text:
A subagent hands back the memo, not the notebook.

Your code asks for a researcher, then an analyst, to assess risk in a contracts folder. The main agent delegates via the Agent tool.

In a fresh context the researcher greps the folder with its own tools. Only its final message returns as the tool result; the Grep calls stay behind, so the main context stays clean.

The takeaway: subagents buy isolation and a focused context. A key idea in the tools domain of the Claude Certified Architect – Foundations (CCAR-F).

Dig into subagents with the CCAR-F prep course and its practice exam:
👉 https://gennoor.com/claude/certifications/architect-foundations

items.title: Tool use: Claude requests, you validate and run
items.text:
Claude does not run your tools. It asks, and your code decides.

An agent asks TicketFlow for the status of alice@example.com. You send the message with a lookup_customer tool and its JSON schema.

Claude does not answer yet: it emits a tool_use block. Your dispatcher validates the email first, returns an error for a malformed one, and only then runs the lookup and sends back the result.

The takeaway: the model requests, your code validates and executes. Tool calling is a full domain of the Claude Certified Developer – Foundations (CCDV-F).

items.title: Iterative refinement: diagnose, revise, verify, decide
items.text:
Eight rewordings later, the bottom line was still buried. Rewording was the problem.

Maya asks Claude for a quarterly client summary, then rewords the request again and again. Versions 6, 7 and 8 all still bury the point.

A colleague asks: did you tell Claude what was wrong? So she switches to a loop: diagnose the draft against her criteria, revise with one targeted follow-up, verify, then decide.

The takeaway: name the problem, do not just rephrase the request. This refinement loop is core to the prompting domain of the Claude Certified Associate – Foundations (CCAS-F).

items.title: HITL gate: human approval before money moves
items.text:
The refund agent proposed $50,000. Ungated, it would simply have paid it.

Week 15: you place can_use_tool between the model's output and any irreversible action.

Over $100, the runtime pauses and the callback posts the exact input to Slack. The manager clicks Approve, the callback returns PermissionResultAllow, and only then does the refund execute.

The takeaway: the gate sits on the action, not on the conversation. Least-privilege agent tooling is a full CCAR-P exam domain.

items.title: Projects: one brief, every chat inherits it
items.text:
Pasting the same 300-word brief into every chat? Write it once instead.

Maya pastes an identical brief into eight client chats in a row. Then she creates a "Quarterly Client Summaries" Project, writes the rules once and uploads the terminology guide.

Every new chat inside the Project inherits the rules and the glossary, so her prompts shrink to what is actually new.

The takeaway: Projects hold shared instructions and knowledge so individual chats do not have to. Expect workspace questions like this on the CCAS-F exam.

items.title: Hooks: deny rm -rf, audit what ran
items.text:
Claude reached for rm -rf. A hook said no before permissions even ran.

Two hooks are registered: PreToolUse on Bash and PostToolUse with no matcher. Asked to clean the build folder, Claude emits rm -rf.

PreToolUse fires before permissions; block_dangerous spots it and denies. The error tells Claude why, so it picks a safe alternative, and PostToolUse audits what actually ran.

The takeaway: hooks are where deterministic policy and auditing live. A heavily weighted CCAR-F topic.

🔊 Turn the sound on for the walkthrough.

items.title: Code Execution: exact numbers, not predictions
items.text:
Claude said "about $47,300". The real total was $44,287.

Maya uploads a 50-row expense sheet and asks for the sum of column D. The estimate is off, and she only finds out by checking by hand.

Her manager explains: a language model predicts text, it does not compute. With Code Execution enabled, Claude writes Python to sum the column and returns the exact figure.

The takeaway: when the answer is a number, have Claude run code rather than guess. A key distinction for the CCAS-F exam, and for anything that reaches finance.

items.topic: Keeping API Keys From the Model
items.title: Secrets & RBAC: the key never reaches Claude
items.text:
If your CRM key is in the system prompt, every trace has a copy.

A billing clerk signs in via SSO and asks about customer C-77. In the wrong design, the CRM key sits in the system prompt, visible to Claude and every log.

The right design sends only the question and tools. When Claude asks for lookup_customer, the handler pulls CRM_API_KEY from Key Vault server-side at execution time.

The takeaway: credentials live with the executor, never in context. A security essential for the Claude Certified Architect – Professional (CCAR-P).

See secrets and RBAC in the CCAR-P prep course, with a practice exam:
👉 https://gennoor.com/claude/certifications/architect-professional

items.title: Format drift: JSON decays until you prune context
items.text:
By turn 15 the JSON quietly lost a field. Lowering temperature will not fix it.

For five turns Claude returns perfect JSON. Then 20+ tool outputs pile up and bury the schema, and the "priority" field goes missing.

The video rules out the tempting fix: temperature tunes randomness, not attention to the schema. The real remedies work on the context itself, including pruning it.

The takeaway: format drift is a context problem. Spotting the wrong fix is exactly what CCDV-F questions test.

🔊 Turn the sound on for the walkthrough.

items.title: Sessions: resume remembers, fork branches
items.text:
Your agent read the report yesterday. Today it remembers nothing, unless you resume.

Turn 1: the agent reads report.md and notes the key numbers. The runtime saves the transcript and your code keeps session_id sess-0001.

Next morning, resume=sess-0001 reloads that history. Skip resume and it is a brand-new session with no memory. fork_session=True branches a copy so you can explore without touching the original.

The takeaway: resume continues, fork branches, nothing persists unless you ask. Classic Claude Certified Architect – Foundations (CCAR-F) material.

👉 https://gennoor.com/claude/certifications/architect-foundations

items.title: Correlation IDs: tracing a failed claim end-to-end
items.text:
"Policy not found." Was it the agent, the retrieval, or the data?

A claims request hits the gateway, which mints a correlation ID. The header carries it to the claims agent, which logs it with the model ID.

Under the same ID, retrieval queries the vector DB and gets zero results; the agent logs it and answers "Policy not found". Every hop exports its spans, so one ID tells the whole story.

The takeaway: one ID across every hop turns guesswork into a trace. Observability sits in the CCAR-P security and compliance domain.

🔊 Turn the sound on for the walkthrough.

items.title: Permission layers: the restart waits for a human
items.text:
No rule blocked the restart. So the decision went to a human.

Told to restart a web service and check its logs, Claude proposes Bash. No hook or deny rule stops it, and no allow rule covers it, so default mode hands it to can_use_tool.

In run 1 the operator declines, and the denial reaches Claude as an error it can work around. The video traces each layer in turn.

The takeaway: when no layer decides, a human does. Tracing which layer fires is a staple of CCAR-F questions.

🔊 Turn the sound on for the walkthrough.

items.title: Memory: Claude remembers the tiers across chats
items.text:
Monday she explained the client tiers. Tuesday, Claude had never heard of them.

Maya walks Claude through Brightline's three client tiers. Next day, in a new chat, Claude has no idea what tier 2 means.

She switches Memory on in Settings and explains the tiers once. Memory keeps those recurring facts, which she can view, edit or delete, and the next chat answers correctly.

The takeaway: chats do not share context by default. Memory is for recurring facts; you stay in control of what is kept. A workspace topic on the Claude Certified Associate – Foundations (CCAS-F).

items.title: Checkpointing: crash at 15, resume at 15
items.text:
A worker crashed at step 15 of 20. Without checkpoints, it starts again at step 1.

Worker A takes a 20-step ticket: classify, research, fix, verify. Workers die mid-task, and with no saves all progress is lost.

So after every step you save the step number, messages and metadata to shared storage. When the worker dies at step 15, the job resumes at step 15.

The takeaway: long agent runs need durable state, not hope. State management is the largest domain on the Claude Certified Developer – Foundations (CCDV-F) exam.

The CCDV-F prep course covers agentic workflows chapter by chapter, with a practice exam:
👉 https://gennoor.com/claude/certifications/developer-foundations

items.title: Model selection: match the model to the task
items.text:
Using the most powerful model for everything is how you burn your rate limit by Wednesday.

Maya sends everything to Opus, including quick policy questions. Her manager sees the usage report: simple tasks are eating the rate limit.

She rematches the work: quick, well-defined lookups move to Haiku, routine weekly summaries to a mid-tier model, and Opus is kept for the tasks that need it.

The takeaway: match the model to the task, not to your habits. Model selection is a recurring CCAS-F exam theme.

items.title: Canary rollout: the gate reverts at 50%
items.text:
The release passed at 5%. It passed at 50%, until it did not.

Week 27: no big-bang release. You arm the rollback gate before any traffic moves, then route the new hybrid retrieval to 5% of clinicians.

After 48 hours the gate checks accuracy and hallucination rate; stage 2 passes too, so the canary widens to 50%. At stage 3 the metrics slip, and the gate reverts automatically.

The takeaway: arm the rollback before the rollout. A defensible-release pattern the Claude Certified Architect – Professional (CCAR-P) expects.

items.title: Orchestrator: split the ticket, merge the results
items.text:
"Charged twice and the app crashes." One agent, two problems, and it lost track.

A mixed billing-and-tech ticket lands, and a single agent forgets which sub-issue it already solved.

You refactor into an orchestrator that splits the ticket into separable sub-tasks and delegates them in parallel. Each specialist gets its own prompt, tools and model, and the orchestrator merges the results.

The takeaway: decompose when the sub-tasks really are separate. A core multi-agent pattern on the CCDV-F exam.

items.title: Structured outputs: typed JSON, not text parsing
items.text:
Still regex-scraping amounts out of an agent's prose? Give it a schema.

Without a schema the agent answers in prose and your code has to parse it. With output_format set to a JSON schema of vendor, amount and due date, the agent knows the shape it must return.

It reads the invoice, the JSON is validated, and the typed object arrives in ResultMessage.structured_output. Repeated failures surface as error_max_structured_output_retries.

The takeaway: typed data in, no text parsing. A practical CCAR-F (Claude Certified Architect – Foundations) topic.

items.title: MCP server: write once, three apps plug in
items.text:
Three teams, the same Jira and CRM tools, three copies drifting apart.

Instead of glue code per app, you build one MCP server exposing jira_create_issue and crm_lookup_customer over JSON-RPC.

TicketFlow calls tools/list and sees each one as mcp__<server>__<tool>. The Escalation Dashboard and Analytics app plug into the same server with no new integration work.

The takeaway: write a tool once and let every client discover it. MCP is a key tool-calling topic for the Claude Certified Developer – Foundations (CCDV-F).

items.title: Task decomposition: three focused prompts beat one
items.text:
"Redesign onboarding" is three jobs hiding in one prompt.

Maya pastes her manager's whole request as one prompt and gets a vague overview. A colleague points out it hides three separate deliverables.

She splits it: prompt 1 asks only for the process map, prompt 2 only for the training plan, and so on, so Claude's full reasoning goes to each piece.

The takeaway: one focused prompt per deliverable beats one prompt for everything. Decomposition sits in the prompting domain of the CCAS-F (Claude Certified Associate – Foundations) exam.

items.title: PreToolUse hook: rm -rf denied before it runs
items.text:
"Be careful" in a prompt is not a safety control. A hook is.

A developer asks Claude Code to wipe a stale build folder and Claude picks rm -rf ./build.

Your .claude/settings.json routes every Bash tool_use to a hook first. check_bash.js reads the command, finds rm -rf and returns deny, so the command never runs.

The takeaway: enforce safety in deterministic code, not in instructions the model may weigh differently. Hooks are core to the CCDV-F Claude Code domain.

items.title: Enterprise patterns: each control in its place
items.text:
bypassPermissions with no isolation is a shortcut you only take once.

The video starts with the shortcut, then puts each control in its place: a sandboxed worker per task with scoped cwd and credentials, a PreToolUse hook that sees sensitive calls first, and can_use_tool parking them in an approval queue.

Once approved, the call goes through a shared MCP server fronting the system, with auditing after the fact.

The takeaway: isolation, hooks, human approval and a governed gateway each do one job. This is the enterprise-scenarios domain of the CCAR-F exam.

items.title: Prompt injection: four layers stop the poisoned ticket
items.text:
An attacker filed a support ticket that said "Ignore previous instructions."

Pasted raw into the prompt, the poisoned ticket almost works. The video then adds defences layer by layer.

Tag the ticket as <user_ticket>, warn in the system prompt that it is untrusted user data, and block the email tool while external input is processed. Claude skips the injected instruction.

The takeaway: no single prompt line stops injection; layers do, and removing the dangerous tool matters most. Expect this on the Claude Certified Developer – Foundations (CCDV-F).

items.title: Data sensitivity: classify, redact, review, then submit
items.text:
Halfway through the summary, she noticed the salaries. Then she stopped.

Maya is drafting a summary from a spreadsheet of employee performance reviews when she spots salaries, manager feedback and accommodation notes.

She checks the HR policy (the answer is a clear no), classifies each field, swaps sensitive values for placeholders, has a peer review the redacted sheet, and only then submits it.

The takeaway: classify, redact, review, submit. Speed never outranks data policy. A must-know sequence for the CCAS-F exam.

items.title: Error routing: 429 warns, 401 pages on-call
items.text:
A 429 and a 401 are both errors. Only one should wake someone up.

TicketFlow runs on BYOC in your AWS account. A retry-loop bug resends a rate-limited call, and 429s start to pile up.

Monitoring groups errors by cause: 429s are rated warn, so the system logs and backs off. An authentication failure is different, and pages on-call.

The takeaway: route errors by what they mean, not by the fact that they failed. Operational judgement like this shows up across the CCDV-F exam.

items.title: can_use_tool: $40 auto-approved, $250 queued
items.text:
$40 refund: approved automatically. $250 refund: denied. Same agent, one callback.

A permission mode is too coarse, so your code sets a can_use_tool callback. Claude is asked to refund two orders.

The $40 refund is under the limit, so the callback returns PermissionResultAllow and issue_refund runs. The $250 one is over the limit and is denied; Claude gets the error and reports back.

The takeaway: can_use_tool lets you decide per call, using the actual input. Expect this pattern on the Claude Certified Architect – Foundations (CCAR-F).

items.title: Hallucination: pinpoint, verify, then regenerate
items.text:
The stat looked perfect for the board slide. The source did not exist.

Maya asks Claude for competitor growth rates and gets a striking figure with three named sources.

She pinpoints the one claim that looks too good, verifies it (one article does not exist, another says 30%, not 300%), then regenerates with a tighter prompt.

The takeaway: pinpoint, verify, regenerate. Confident citations are not checked citations. Discernment like this is central to the Claude Certified Associate – Foundations (CCAS-F).

items.topic: Built-in, SDK and External MCP Tools
items.title: Tools compared: same gate, different process boundary
items.text:
Built-in, in-process or external MCP: same gate, different process boundary.

Claude reads a file with a built-in tool. Then it calls your @tool for a business system, which runs in-process via an SDK MCP server so the logic stays private. A shared third-party capability comes from an external MCP server instead.

All three pass the same permission gate and use the same tool-use protocol. What changes is where the code runs.

The takeaway: pick a tool type by where the logic should live. A common CCAR-F comparison question.
